hmmt-feb-2005-guts-01.title: Divisibility
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-01.body:
The condition is $\frac{n(n+1)}2\ \Big|\ \frac{n^2(n^2+1)}2$, i.e. $n+1\mid n(n^2+1)=n^3+n$. Since $n+1\mid(n+1)(n^2-n+2)=n^3+n+2$, we need $n+1\mid2$, so $n\le1$. And $n=1$ works.

**Answer: 1**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-02.title: AM-GM
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-02.body:
Expanding, $xy+z=xy+xz+yz+z^2$, so $z^2+(x+y-1)z=0$. As $z>0$, $z=1-x-y$, i.e. $x+y+z=1$. By AM-GM $xyz\le\left(\frac{x+y+z}3\right)^3=\frac1{27}$, with equality at $x=y=z=\frac13$.

**Answer: $\tfrac1{27}$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-03.title: Telescoping
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-03.body:
For $m=2^k$: $\frac{2^m}{4^m-1}=\frac{(2^m+1)-1}{(2^m-1)(2^m+1)}=\frac1{2^m-1}-\frac1{4^m-1}$. With $m=2^k$ we have $4^m-1=2^{2m}-1$, which is the next term's $2^{m'}-1$ with $m'=2m$. So the sum is $\sum_{k\ge0}\left(\frac1{2^{2^k}-1}-\frac1{2^{2^{k+1}}-1}\right)=\frac1{2^1-1}-0=1$.

**Answer: 1**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-04.title: Inclusion-exclusion
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-04.body:
There are $\frac{8!}{2!\,2!}=10080$ distinct arrangements (two $M$'s and two $0$'s repeat). To read “HMMT” we pick $4$ positions for the letters ($\binom84=70$ ways, arranged in the order H,M,M,T); the digits $2,0,0,5$ fill the remaining spots in $\frac{4!}{2}=12$ ways: $70\cdot12=840$. The same for “2005”: $840$. Both can be read exactly when the letters occupy some $4$ positions in order H,M,M,T and the digits the other $4$ in the order $2,0,0,5$: $\binom84=70$ arrangements. So the count is $840+840-70=1610$ and the probability is $\frac{1610}{10080}=\frac{23}{144}$.

**Answer: $\tfrac{23}{144}$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-05.title: It is always divisible
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-05.body:
$2\cdot6\cdots(4n-2)=2^n\cdot1\cdot3\cdots(2n-1)=\frac{2^n\cdot(2n)!}{2\cdot4\cdots2n}=\frac{(2n)!}{n!}$. Then $\frac{(2n)!}{n!\cdot n!}=\binom{2n}n$ is an integer, so $n!$ always divides the product. All $2005$ integers work.

**Answer: 2005**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-06.title: Hit the value 2
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-06.body:
For any $m$, $m\circ2=\frac{m+2}{2m+4}=\frac12$. So when the operation reaches $\cdots\circ2$, the running value becomes $\frac12$. Then $\frac12\circ1=\frac{3/2}{1/2+4}=\frac13$, and $\frac13\circ0=\frac{1/3}4=\frac1{12}$.

**Answer: $\tfrac1{12}$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-07.title: Collinear heads
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-07.body:
Put the people on the $x$-axis; the head tops lie on a line $y=mx+c$. The $k$-th person stands at $x_k$ with height $h_k=mx_k+c$, and the next person stands at $x_{k+1}=x_k+h_k$. Hence
$$h_{k+1}=mx_{k+1}+c=h_k+mh_k=(1+m)h_k.$$
So the five heights form a geometric progression, and the middle height is the geometric mean of the shortest and tallest: $\sqrt{3\cdot7}=\sqrt{21}$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{21}$ feet**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-08.title: Area ratio
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-08.body:
Since $\angle A$ and $\angle C$ of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, $\sin A=\sin C$, so
$$\frac{[BCD]}{[ABD]}=\frac{\frac12BC\cdot CD\sin C}{\frac12DA\cdot AB\sin A}=\frac{BC\cdot CD}{DA\cdot AB}.$$
The other three sides are distinct integers larger than $AB$ and at most $10$, so $AB\le7$.
- $AB=7$: the other sides are $8,9,10$ in some order, and $7\nmid BC\cdot CD$, so the ratio is not an integer.
- $AB=6$: we need $6\,DA\mid BC\cdot CD$ with $\{DA,BC,CD\}\subset\{7,8,9,10\}$. For $DA=7,8,9,10$ the products $BC\cdot CD$ available are $\{72,80,90\}$, $\{63,70,90\}$, $\{56,70,80\}$, $\{56,63,72\}$, and none is divisible by $42,48,54,60$ respectively.
- $AB=5$: $BC=10$, $CD=9$, $DA=6$ gives $\frac{90}{6\cdot5}=3$. A cyclic quadrilateral with sides $5,10,9,6$ exists because each side is less than the sum of the other three.

So the largest $AB$ is $5$.

**Answer: 5**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-09.title: Count protected ducks
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-09.body:
Let there be $c$ cows and $r$ rabbits, $c+r=400$. Each cow protects at most $2$ ducks (its neighbors): at most $2c$ ducks. A duck between two rabbits is determined by a pair of rabbits at distance $2$; each rabbit is in at most two such “rabbit-duck-rabbit” triples, so there are at most $r$ such ducks, and equality would force the circle to alternate rabbit, duck, rabbit, duck throughout, impossible with $600>500$ ducks; so at most $r-1$. Therefore $600\le(r-1)+2c=(400-c)-1+2c=399+c$, so $c\ge201$.

An arrangement with $201$ cows exists. Going around the circle: a block $R\,D\,R\,D\cdots D\,R$ ($199$ rabbits, $198$ ducks, every duck between two rabbits), followed by $201$ blocks $D\,C\,D$ (cow with a duck on each side). That is $199+198+201+402=1000$ animals, $600$ ducks and $201$ cows, and every duck is either between two rabbits or next to a cow (the first and last ducks of the cow part are next to a cow too).

**Answer: 201**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-10.title: At most 8, with a construction
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-10.body:
In a pile $\{a,b,ab\}$, the two factors cannot both be $\ge10$ (the product would exceed $100$: $10\cdot11>100$), and $1$ cannot occur (the other two cards would be equal). So every pile uses one of $2,3,\dots,9$ as a factor, and each of these cards is in at most one pile: at most $8$ piles.

Eight piles exist: $\{2,18,36\},\{3,17,51\},\{4,16,64\},\{5,15,75\},\{6,14,84\},\{7,13,91\},\{8,12,96\},\{9,11,99\}$.

**Answer: 8**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-11.title: Staircase argument
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-11.body:
The patches west and south of an Ann patch $P$ are Ann's, so $P$ can have two Keith neighbors only if the patches north and east of $P$ both exist and belong to Keith. Hence $P$ is the topmost Ann patch of its column and the easternmost of its row. In particular the scarecrow patches lie in distinct columns and distinct rows.

Let there be $n$ scarecrows, in rows $r_1<\dots<r_n$ (counted from the south). In the column of the scarecrow in row $r_i$, Ann farms all $r_i$ patches up to that one, and the columns are different. So Ann farms at least $r_1+\cdots+r_n\ge1+2+\cdots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}2$ patches. Since $\frac{8\cdot9}2=36>30$, $n\le7$.

$n=7$ is possible: let Ann farm the western columns $1,\dots,7$ up to heights $9,6,5,4,3,2,1$ (that is $30$ patches) and Keith everything else. The top patch of each of these seven columns has a Keith patch to its north and to its east, and no other Ann patch has two Keith neighbors.

**Answer: 7**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-12.title: Three cases for the given pair
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-12.body:
Let $P,Q$ be the given vertices, at distance $1$. They can be (i) adjacent, (ii) opposite corners of a face, or (iii) opposite corners of the cube. Rotating the cube about the line $PQ$, each of the other vertices traces a circle around that axis, and vertices related by the rotation symmetry trace the same circle.

(i) Adjacent (cube side $1$): the two other vertices adjacent to $P$ trace one circle of radius $1$ centered at $P$; the two adjacent to $Q$ trace one circle of radius $1$ centered at $Q$; the vertex at distance $\sqrt2$ from $P$ traces a circle of radius $\sqrt2$ centered at $P$, and the one at distance $\sqrt2$ from $Q$ traces a circle of radius $\sqrt2$ centered at $Q$. That is $4$ circles.

(ii) Face diagonal (cube side $\frac1{\sqrt2}$): the two vertices adjacent to both $P$ and $Q$ trace one circle of radius $\frac12$; the vertex adjacent to only $P$ and the one adjacent to only $Q$ trace two circles of radius $\frac{\sqrt2}2$; the two vertices adjacent to neither trace one circle of radius $\frac{\sqrt3}2$. That is $4$ circles.

(iii) Space diagonal (cube side $\frac1{\sqrt3}$): the three vertices adjacent to $P$ trace one circle of radius $\frac{\sqrt2}3$ and the three adjacent to $Q$ trace another. That is $2$ circles.

All these circles are different, so $n=4+4+2=10$.

**Answer: 10**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-13.title: Law of cosines twice
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-13.body:
By the Law of Cosines, $\cos\angle BAC=\frac{1+3-7}{2\sqrt3}=-\frac{\sqrt3}2$, so $\angle BAC=150^\circ$. Let $Q$ be where $\ell_2$ meets line $AC$. In right triangle $ABQ$ (right angle at $Q$) with $\angle QAB=30^\circ$ (the supplement of $150^\circ$), $\angle ABQ=60^\circ$. Since $PA\perp AB$, triangle $ABP$ has a right angle at $A$ and $\angle ABP=60^\circ$, so $PB=2$, $PA=\sqrt3$. The angle $\angle PAC=360^\circ-90^\circ-150^\circ=120^\circ$, so
$$PC^2=PA^2+AC^2-2\,PA\cdot AC\cos120^\circ=3+3+3=9,\quad PC=3.$$

**Answer: 3**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-14.title: Parabolas with a given axis direction
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-14.body:
Let $m$ be a line perpendicular to $\ell$. The circle centered at $P_i$ tangent to $m$ has radius $d(P_i,m)$. The three circles pass through a common point $F$ exactly when $FP_i=d(P_i,m)$ for $i=1,2,3$, i.e. when all three points lie on the parabola with focus $F$ and directrix $m$. Such a parabola has axis perpendicular to $m$, i.e. parallel to $\ell$.

Choose coordinates with $\ell$ the $x$-axis, so $m$ is a vertical line $x=k$ and the parabola has a horizontal axis: it is $x=ay^2+by+c$ with $a\ne0$. Conversely, every such parabola has exactly one focus and one directrix, and the directrix is a vertical line. No two of the points lie on a horizontal line, so they have three distinct $y$-coordinates and exactly one quadratic polynomial $x=ay^2+by+c$ passes through them (Lagrange interpolation); its leading coefficient $a$ is nonzero because the points are not collinear. So there is exactly one such parabola, hence exactly one line $m$. Therefore $n=1$ always.

**Answer: 1**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-15.title: Boundary points of the hull
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-15.body:
$S$ consists of the lattice points with $x^2+y^2\le10$. The convex hull of $S$ is an octagon with vertices $(\pm1,\pm3)$, $(\pm3,\pm1)$; the lattice points on its boundary are these eight together with $(0,\pm3),(\pm3,0),(\pm2,\pm2)$: $16$ points. A triangle of maximum area has its vertices on the boundary of the hull (moving a vertex outward in the direction of the perpendicular to the opposite side cannot decrease the area, and a vertex not on the hull boundary can be moved to the boundary). Checking the $\binom{16}3$ triangles with vertices among these $16$ points, the maximum area is $M=12$ (it is below $13$, the area of an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle of radius $\sqrt{10}$, and the areas are multiples of $\frac12$).

The triangles of area $12$ fall into three classes under the symmetries of the square (reflections and rotations), with representatives
- $(2,2),(1,-3),(-3,1)$ (orbit of size $4$),
- $(3,-1),(-3,-1),(1,3)$ (orbit of size $8$),
- $(3,-1),(-3,-1),(0,3)$ (orbit of size $4$),

for a total of $4+8+4=16$ triangles.

**Answer: 16**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-16.title: Coordinates
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-16.body:
Place the octahedron with vertices $(\pm a,0,0),(0,\pm a,0),(0,0,\pm a)$. An edge has length $a\sqrt2=1$, so $a=\frac1{\sqrt2}$. Two opposite faces lie in the parallel planes $x+y+z=a$ and $x+y+z=-a$. Their distance is $\frac{2a}{\sqrt3}=\frac{2}{\sqrt2\sqrt3}=\frac{2}{\sqrt6}=\frac{\sqrt6}3$.

**Answer: $\tfrac{\sqrt6}3$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-17.title: Take logarithms
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-17.body:
Let the value be $2^L$. Taking $\log_2$ of the nested expression gives
$$L=1+\frac12\left(1+\frac13\left(1+\frac14\left(1+\cdots\right)\right)\right)=1+\frac1{2}+\frac1{2\cdot3}+\frac1{2\cdot3\cdot4}+\cdots=\frac1{1!}+\frac1{2!}+\frac1{3!}+\frac1{4!}+\cdots=e-1.$$
So the value is $2^{e-1}$.

**Answer: $2^{e-1}$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-18.title: Add a fourth variable
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-18.body:
Let $d$ be a fourth independent uniform number. For fixed $a,b,c$, the probability that $d<\min(a,b,c)$ equals $\min(a,b,c)$. Averaging, $E[\min(a,b,c)]=P(d<\min(a,b,c))=P(d\text{ is the smallest of the four})=\frac14$ by symmetry.

**Answer: $\tfrac14$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-19.title: The degenerate limiting case
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-19.body:
The quadrilateral is a kite, so its diagonals $A'C'$ and $B'D'$ are perpendicular and its area is $\frac12A'C'\cdot B'D'$. The upper end $b$ of the interval corresponds to the limiting position in which the kite degenerates into an isosceles triangle, which happens when the altitude from $A$ to face $BCD$ is parallel to the projection plane. Let $s$ be the edge length. The altitude from $A$ meets the center of face $BCD$ and has length $\sqrt{s^2-\frac{s^2}3}=\frac{s\sqrt6}3$, which projects without shrinking, so $A'C'=\frac{s\sqrt6}3$ in this limit; $BD$ is also parallel to the plane, so $B'D'=s$. The area is $\frac12\cdot\frac{s\sqrt6}3\cdot s=\frac{s^2\sqrt6}6$. Setting it to $4$: $s^2=4\sqrt6$, so $b=s=2\sqrt[4]6$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt[4]{6}$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-20.title: Digits must share a factor
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-20.body:
Let $n=xy$ be a zesty two-digit number. If $x,y$ were both one-digit, then $s(x)s(y)=xy=n\ne s(n)$. So one of them, say $x=10a+b$, has two digits; then $y\le9$ and $s(y)=y$. Now $n=10(ay)+by$, and
$$s(n)\le s(ay)+s(by)\le ay+by=y\,(a+b)=s(y)s(x),$$
with equality only if $ay\le9$ and $by\le9$ (no carries). So the condition forces the two digits of $n$ to be $ay$ and $by$: both are divisible by $y>1$. Conversely, if the digits $p,q$ of $n$ are both multiples of some $y\ge2$, say $p=ay$, $q=by$, then $x=10a+b$ gives $xy=n$ and $s(x)s(y)=(a+b)y=p+q=s(n)$.

So we count two-digit numbers $\overline{pq}$ whose digits (with $0$ divisible by everything) have a common divisor greater than $1$. By tens digit $p=2,\dots,9$ the numbers of allowed $q\in\{0,\dots,9\}$ are $5,4,5,2,7,2,5,4$ (for $p=1$ there are none). The total is $34$.

**Answer: 34**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-21.title: Tangent subtraction/addition
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-21.body:
Let $h=AD$. There are two positions of $D$ relative to $B,C$.

*$D$ between $B$ and $C$:* $\angle BAC=\arctan\frac3h+\arctan\frac2h=45^\circ$, so $\dfrac{\frac3h+\frac2h}{1-\frac6{h^2}}=1$, i.e. $5h=h^2-6$, so $h=6$ (taking the positive root).

*$D$ outside $BC$* ($C$ between $D$ and $B$): $\angle BAC=\arctan\frac3h-\arctan\frac2h=45^\circ$ gives $\frac{h}{h^2+6}=1$, i.e. $h^2-h+6=0$, which has no real solution.

So $h=6$, $BC=5$, and the area is $\frac12\cdot5\cdot6=15$.

**Answer: 15**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-22.title: Fractional parts and a product
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-22.body:
$\ln(1+e^{2^k})=2^k+\ln(1+e^{-2^k})$ and $0<\ln(1+e^{-2^k})\le\ln(1+e^{-1})<1$, so $\{\ln(1+e^{2^k})\}=\ln(1+e^{-2^k})$. With $x=e^{-1}$ the sum is $\ln\prod_{k\ge0}(1+x^{2^k})$. Since $\prod_{k=0}^{n}(1+x^{2^k})=1+x+x^2+\cdots+x^{2^{n+1}-1}$ (each integer below $2^{n+1}$ has a unique binary expansion), the infinite product equals $\frac1{1-x}$ for $|x|<1$. So the sum is
$$\ln\frac1{1-e^{-1}}=\ln\frac{e}{e-1}=1-\ln(e-1).$$

**Answer: $1-\ln(e-1)$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-23.title: Similar triangles
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-23.body:
Take the hexagon with side $3$; then $A_1,A_4,A_7,\dots$ are the vertices, and $A_5$ is the trisection point of side $A_4A_7$ nearest to $A_4$. In triangle $A_1A_4A_5$: $A_1A_4=3$, $A_4A_5=1$, $\angle A_1A_4A_5=120^\circ$, so $A_1A_5=\sqrt{9+1+3}=\sqrt{13}$.

Let $P$ be the intersection of $A_1A_5$ with the next segment $A_4A_8$ (a vertex of the inner region). By symmetry $\angle A_4A_1A_5=\angle A_5A_4P$, so triangles $A_1A_4A_5$ and $A_4PA_5$ are similar, giving $PA_5=\frac{A_4A_5^2}{A_1A_5}=\frac1{\sqrt{13}}$. Let $Q$ be the intersection of $A_1A_5$ with the previous segment $A_{16}A_2$; the same reasoning gives $A_1Q=\frac3{\sqrt{13}}$ by symmetry. Then
$$PQ=A_1A_5-A_1Q-PA_5=\sqrt{13}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}-\frac1{\sqrt{13}}=\frac9{\sqrt{13}}.$$
By symmetry the region is a regular hexagon of side $\frac9{\sqrt{13}}$, while the large hexagon has side $3$. The area ratio is $\left(\frac{9/\sqrt{13}}3\right)^2=\frac9{13}$.

**Answer: $\tfrac9{13}$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-24.title: Column analysis
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-24.body:
A sum of two $4$-digit numbers is below $20000$, so $R=1$. Let $c_1,c_2,c_3$ be the carries out of the units, tens and hundreds columns. The hundreds column reads $M+U+c_2=U+10c_3$, so either $M=0,\ c_2=c_3=0$ or $M=9,\ c_2=c_3=1$. The thousands column reads $H+G+c_3=10+O$.

**$O=7$ is impossible.** Then $H+G=17+\ldots$: $H+G+c_3=17$ forces $\{H,G\}=\{8,9\}$, so $M\ne9$, $M=0$, $c_2=c_3=0$. The tens column gives $N=T+c_1$, so $c_1=1$ and $N=T+1$, and the units column $T+S=D+10$. The digits left for $T,U,S,N,D$ are $2,3,4,5,6$, so $T+S\le 6+5=11$ and $D=T+S-10\le1$, a contradiction.

**$O=6$:** 
- If $M=9$ ($c_2=c_3=1$): $H+G=15$ gives $\{H,G\}=\{7,8\}$ and the digits $0,2,3,4,5$ remain for $T,U,S,N,D$. The tens column gives $N=T+c_1-1$; $c_1=1$ would give $N=T$, so $c_1=0$, $N=T-1$ and $D=T+S$. The possibilities $(N,T)=(2,3),(3,4),(4,5)$ leave no valid $S,D$ (one checks each in a line).
- If $M=0$ ($c_2=c_3=0$): $H+G=16$ gives $\{H,G\}=\{7,9\}$ and $2,3,4,5,8$ remain for $T,U,S,N,D$. Again $c_1=1$, $N=T+1$, $D=T+S-10$, so $T+S\ge12$: the pairs from $\{2,3,4,5,8\}$ are $\{4,8\}$ or $\{5,8\}$; $T=8$ would give $N=9$ (used), $T=5$ gives $N=6$ (used), so $T=4$, $S=8$, $N=5$, $D=2$, $U=3$.

Thus $ROUND=16352$, e.g. $7004+9348=16352$ (also $9004+7348$). Since $O\le6$ and $O=6$ forces this, it is the maximum.

**Answer: 16352**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-25.title: Recurrence
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-25.body:
Let $p_n$ be the probability the ant is at the start vertex after $n$ minutes; $p_0=1$. After $n$ minutes it is at each of the other three vertices with probability $\frac{1-p_n}3$, and from each of those it returns to the start with probability $\frac13$. So $p_{n+1}=\frac{1-p_n}3$. Put $q_n=p_n-\frac14$: then $q_{n+1}=-\frac13q_n$, $q_0=\frac34$, so $q_n=\frac34\left(-\frac13\right)^n$. Hence
$$p_{60}=\frac14+\frac34\cdot\frac1{3^{60}}=\frac14+\frac1{4\cdot3^{59}}=\frac{3^{59}+1}{4\cdot3^{59}}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{3^{59}+1}{4\cdot3^{59}}$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-26.title: Show $D$ is the midpoint of $AE$
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-26.body:
By the Angle Bisector Theorem, $\frac{DC}{DB}=\frac{AC}{AB}=3$. Extend $CE$ to meet line $AB$ at $F$. Since $AE$ bisects $\angle A$ and is perpendicular to $CF$, triangle $ACF$ is isosceles: $AF=AC=3AB$ and $E$ is the midpoint of $CF$. Let $G$ be the midpoint of $BF$. Then $BF=2AB$, so $BG=AB$, i.e. $B$ is the midpoint of $AG$. Also $GE\parallel BC$ (midline of triangle $FBC$). In triangle $AGE$, $B$ is the midpoint of $AG$ and $BD\parallel GE$, so $D$ is the midpoint of $AE$: $AD=DE$.

The angles $\angle ADB$ and $\angle EDC$ are vertical, so
$$\frac{[ABD]}{[CDE]}=\frac{\frac12AD\cdot BD\sin\angle ADB}{\frac12DE\cdot DC\sin\angle EDC}=\frac{AD}{DE}\cdot\frac{BD}{DC}=1\cdot\frac13=\frac13.$$

**Answer: $\tfrac13$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-27.title: Counting argument and an example
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-27.body:
Take any five players. Consider all ordered triples $(A,B,C)$ of distinct players among them: there are $5\cdot4\cdot3=60$, and each one has exactly one true statement. Count pairs “$X$ takes lessons from $Y$” (say there are $L$ of them among the five players). Each such pair makes exactly one statement true in each ordered triple in which it appears as “$A$ takes from $B$”, “$B$ takes from $C$” or “$C$ takes from $A$”: there are $3$ choices of the third player and $3$ positions, so $9$ ordered triples. Thus $9L=60$, impossible. So there cannot be $5$ (or more) players.

Four players are possible: $P,Q,R,S$ with $P,Q$ taking lessons from each other, $R,S$ taking lessons from each other, and no other lessons. For any triple, two of the people belong to one pair and the third to the other pair (or ... every triple contains exactly one of the mutual pairs and one outsider), and checking the three statements shows exactly one is true.

**Answer: 4**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-28.title: A cubic in $t=x/y$
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-28.body:
From $2004(x^3-3xy^2)=2005(y^3-3x^2y)$, dividing by $y^3$ (note $y\ne0$) and setting $t=\frac xy$:
$$2004(t^3-3t)-2005(1-3t^2)=0,\quad\text{i.e. } P(t)=2004t^3+6015t^2-6012t-2005=0.$$
Each solution pair gives a root $t_i=x_i/y_i$ of $P$; $P(-4)<0<P(-3)$, $P(-3)>0>P(0)$, $P(0)<0<P(1)$ so $P$ has three real roots, which must be the three $t_i$. Then $P(t)=2004(t-t_1)(t-t_2)(t-t_3)$, and
$$\prod(1-t_i)=\frac{P(1)}{2004}=\frac{2004+6015-6012-2005}{2004}=\frac2{2004}=\frac1{1002}.$$

**Answer: $\tfrac1{1002}$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-29.title: Count colorings by number of colors used
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-29.body:
Count colorings up to rotation by the number of colors used:
- $4$ colors: there are two mirror-image colorings for each set of $4$ colors: $2\binom n4$.
- $3$ colors: one color is used twice (it determines the coloring): $3\binom n3$.
- $2$ colors: either one color on $3$ faces and the other on $1$ face ($2$ ways), or $2+2$ ($1$ way): $3\binom n2$.
- $1$ color: $\binom n1$.

Total: $2\binom n4+3\binom n3+3\binom n2+n=\frac{n^2(n^2+11)}{12}$. Setting this equal to $n^3$: $n^2(n^2+11)=12n^3$, so $n^2(n-1)(n-11)=0$. Since $n>0$: $n=1$ or $n=11$.

**Answer: $n=1$ or $n=11$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-30.title: Cut corners off a cube
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-30.body:
The vertices of the cuboctahedron are the midpoints of the edges of a cube of side $s$, so the cuboctahedron is the cube with the eight corner tetrahedra cut off. Each cut tetrahedron has a right-isosceles base of legs $\frac s2$ (area $\frac12\left(\frac s2\right)^2$) and height $\frac s2$, so its volume is $\frac13\cdot\frac12\left(\frac s2\right)^2\cdot\frac s2=\frac{(s/2)^3}6$. The volume is $s^3-8\cdot\frac{s^3}{48}=\frac56s^3$.

An edge of the cuboctahedron joins midpoints of two adjacent edges of the cube, so it is the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle with legs $\frac s2$: $1=\frac s2\sqrt2$, $s=\sqrt2$. The volume is $\frac56(\sqrt2)^3=\frac{5\sqrt2}3$.

**Answer: $\tfrac{5\sqrt2}3$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-31.title: Track the four orientations
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-31.body:
After $n$ subdivisions let $a_n,b_n,c_n,d_n$ be the numbers of small L's with the original orientation and rotated by $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$, $270^\circ$ respectively. Subdividing one L produces two L's of the same orientation, one of each neighboring orientation, and none of the opposite orientation. Therefore
$$(a_{n+1},b_{n+1},c_{n+1},d_{n+1})=(d_n+2a_n+b_n,\ a_n+2b_n+c_n,\ b_n+2c_n+d_n,\ c_n+2d_n+a_n).$$
Starting from $(a_0,b_0,c_0,d_0)=(1,0,0,0)$ we get $(a_1,\dots)=(2,1,0,1)$, and by induction
$$(a_n,b_n,c_n,d_n)=\left(4^{n-1}+2^{n-1},\ 4^{n-1},\ 4^{n-1}-2^{n-1},\ 4^{n-1}\right)\quad(n\ge1).$$
(The inductive step: $a_{n+1}=4^{n-1}+2(4^{n-1}+2^{n-1})+4^{n-1}=4^n+2^n$, $b_{n+1}=4^{n-1}+2^{n-1}+2\cdot4^{n-1}+4^{n-1}-2^{n-1}=4^n$, and similarly for the others.) So after $2005$ subdivisions the number of L's with the original orientation is $a_{2005}=4^{2004}+2^{2004}$.

**Answer: $4^{2004}+2^{2004}$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-32.title: Closed form and Wilson's theorem
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-32.body:
We claim $a_n=2\cdot n!+1$: it holds for $n=1$, and $(n+1)(2\cdot n!+1)-n=2\cdot(n+1)!+1$. Then $a_{m+1}-1=2(m+1)!$ and $a_m^2-1=(a_m-1)(a_m+1)=2\,m!\cdot(2\,m!+2)=4\,m!\,(m!+1)$. The condition $2(m+1)!\mid4\,m!\,(m!+1)$ is equivalent to $m+1\mid2(m!+1)$.

If $m+1$ were composite (and $m+1\ge2006$), it would have a proper divisor $d>2$; then $d\mid m!$, and $d\mid2(m!+1)$ would give $d\mid2$, a contradiction. So $m+1$ is prime, and conversely for prime $m+1$, Wilson's theorem gives $m!\equiv-1\pmod{m+1}$, so the condition holds. We need the smallest prime $m+1\ge2006$: $2006,2007=3^2\cdot223,2008,2009=7^2\cdot41,2010$ are composite and $2011$ is prime. So $m=2010$.

**Answer: 2010**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-33.title: Antipodes
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-33.body:
The reflection $A_2$ of $A_1$ over the midpoint of $BC$ is the point where the $A$-excircle touches $BC$. The homothety centered at $A$ taking the excircle to $\omega$ sends $A_2$ to the point of $\omega$ whose tangent is parallel to $BC$ on the side closer to $A$; that is the point $A_3$ of $AA_2\cap\omega$ nearer to $A$, and it is the antipode of $A_1$ on $\omega$. Similarly $B_3,C_3$ are the antipodes of $B_1,C_1$. So $A_3B_3C_3$ is the reflection of $A_1B_1C_1$ through the incenter, and the two triangles are congruent. It remains to find $[A_1B_1C_1]/[ABC]$.

The semiperimeter is $16$, so the tangent lengths are $s-a=6$ (from $A$), $s-b=3$ (from $B$), $s-c=7$ (from $C$), where $a=10,b=13,c=9$. Then
$$\frac{[A_1BC_1]}{[ABC]}=\frac{3\cdot3}{9\cdot10}=\frac1{10},\quad\frac{[A_1B_1C]}{[ABC]}=\frac{7\cdot7}{10\cdot13}=\frac{49}{130},\quad\frac{[AB_1C_1]}{[ABC]}=\frac{6\cdot6}{9\cdot13}=\frac4{13}.$$
Therefore $\frac{[A_1B_1C_1]}{[ABC]}=1-\frac1{10}-\frac{49}{130}-\frac4{13}=\frac{14}{65}$.

**Answer: $\tfrac{14}{65}$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-34.title: Coordinates
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-34.body:
Put $A=(1,0,0)$, $D=(-1,0,0)$, $B=(0,1,0)$, $E=(0,-1,0)$, $C=(0,0,1)$, $F=(0,0,-1)$. Then
$$G=\Big(\tfrac1{1+\rho},\tfrac\rho{1+\rho},0\Big),\ H=\Big(0,\tfrac1{1+\rho},\tfrac\rho{1+\rho}\Big),\ I=\Big(\tfrac\rho{1+\rho},0,\tfrac1{1+\rho}\Big),$$
and $GH^2=HI^2=IG^2=\frac{1+(\rho-1)^2+\rho^2}{(1+\rho)^2}=\frac{2\rho^2-2\rho+2}{(1+\rho)^2}$.

Another face $HIJ$ of the icosahedron has its third vertex $J$ on edge $CE$ with $\frac{EJ}{JC}=\rho$: $J=\big(0,-\frac1{1+\rho},\frac\rho{1+\rho}\big)$. Then $HJ^2=\frac4{(1+\rho)^2}$. Equal edges require $HJ=HI$: $4=2\rho^2-2\rho+2$, so $\rho^2-\rho-1=0$ and $\rho=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$ (the golden ratio, as expected for an icosahedron).

**Answer: $\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}2$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-35.title: Pythagorean triples
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-35.body:
The quadratics $\pm x^2\pm px\pm c$ have discriminants $p^2\pm4c$ (the discriminant of $\epsilon_1x^2+\epsilon_2px+\epsilon_3c$ is $p^2-4\epsilon_1\epsilon_3c$). All have rational roots iff both $p^2+4c=a^2$ and $p^2-4c=b^2$ are perfect squares, with $a>b\ge0$ (as $c>0$). Then $a^2+b^2=2p^2$, and $a,b$ have the same parity, so with $u=\frac{a+b}2$ and $v=\frac{a-b}2$ we get $u^2+v^2=\frac{a^2+b^2}2=p^2$, where $u,v$ are positive integers ($v>0$ because $c>0$ gives $a>b$, and $u>0$ because $a>0$).

But $p=2^{24036583}-1\equiv3\pmod4$ is prime, and a prime $\equiv3\pmod4$ dividing $u^2+v^2$ must divide both $u$ and $v$ (since $-1$ is not a quadratic residue mod $p$). Then $p\mid u,v$ and $u^2+v^2=p^2$ forces one of them to be $0$, contradiction. So there is no such $c$.

**Answer: 0**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-36.title: Distribution of the number seated
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-36.body:
Number the seats $1,\dots,100$ starting from the far-right (entrance) seat, and let $s_i$ be the favorite seat of the $i$-th person to enter ($s_i$ uniform on $\{1,\dots,100\}$, independent). If $m$ is the lowest-numbered occupied seat, person $i$ sits in seat $\min(s_i,m-1)$, and cannot sit in the first row if this is $0$. So with $m_i$ the lowest occupied seat after person $i$ ($m_0=101$), $m_i=\min(s_i,m_{i-1}-1)$, and
$$m_n=\min\big(s_n,\ s_{n-1}-1,\ \dots,\ s_1-(n-1)\big).$$
At least $n$ people sit iff $m_n\ge1$, i.e. $s_1\ge n,\ s_2\ge n-1,\ \dots,\ s_n\ge1$. This has probability
$$P(n)=\frac{101-n}{100}\cdot\frac{102-n}{100}\cdots\frac{100}{100}=\frac{100!}{(100-n)!\,100^n}.$$
The probability of exactly $n$ is $Q(n)=P(n)-P(n+1)=\frac{100!\,n}{(100-n)!\,100^{n+1}}$, and
$$\frac{Q(n)}{Q(n-1)}=\frac{n(101-n)}{100(n-1)}>1\iff n^2-n-100<0\iff n\le10.$$
So $Q$ increases up to $n=10$ and decreases after; the most likely number is $10$.

**Answer: 10**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-37.title: A clever polynomial
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-37.body:
Let $q(x)=\dfrac{x(x-2)(x-3)\cdots(x-2005)}{2004!}=\sum_{n=1}^{2005}c_nx^n$. It has zero constant term, roots $0,2,3,\dots,2005$, leading coefficient $c_{2005}=\frac1{2004!}$, and
$$q(1)=\frac{(-1)(-2)\cdots(-2004)}{2004!}=1.$$
Multiply the $n$-th equation by $c_n$ and add them all ($n=1,\dots,2005$). The left side becomes $\sum_i a_i\sum_nc_ni^n=\sum_ia_iq(i)=a_1q(1)=a_1$. The right side is $c_{2005}\cdot1=\frac1{2004!}$ (all the other equations have right side $0$). So $a_1=\frac1{2004!}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac1{2004!}$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-38.title: Orbits of two rotations
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-38.body:
The map $\varphi_1(a,b)=(-1-b,a+1)$ is the $90^\circ$ counterclockwise rotation about $(-1,0)$, and $\varphi_2(a,b)=(1-b,a-1)$ is the $90^\circ$ counterclockwise rotation about $(1,0)$. A coloring is allowed iff each point has the same color as its image under both rotations, i.e. iff every orbit of the group $G$ generated by $\varphi_1,\varphi_2$ is monochromatic. The number of colorings is $2^{\#\text{orbits}}$.

Since $\varphi_1(1,0)=(-1,2)$, composing rotations shows that $G$ contains the $90^\circ$ rotation about every point $(x,y)$ with $x$ odd and $y$ even. The orbits are the four sets
$L_1=\{x+y\equiv0\ (2)\}$, $L_2=\{x\equiv y-1\equiv0\ (2)\}$, $L_3=\{x+y-1\equiv y-x+1\equiv0\ (4)\}$, $L_4=\{x+y+1\equiv y-x-1\equiv0\ (4)\}$:
within each of them any point can be carried to any other by these rotations, and the rotations never leave the set. (A computer check of the connected pieces of the orbit graph on a large grid also gives four classes.) So there are $4$ orbits and $2^4=16$ colorings.

**Answer: 16**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-39.title: Polar form
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-39.body:
Group the terms: $(x^6+3x^4y^2+3x^2y^4+y^6)-(x^5-10x^3y^2+5xy^4)=(x^2+y^2)^3-\operatorname{Re}\big((x+iy)^5\big)$, because $(x+iy)^5=x^5+5ix^4y-10x^3y^2-10ix^2y^3+5xy^4+iy^5$. In polar coordinates the equation is $r^6-r^5\cos5\theta=0$, i.e. $r=0$ or $r=\cos5\theta$. The curve $r=\cos5\theta$ is a five-petal rose, and it passes through the origin. The bounded regions are the interiors of the $5$ petals.

**Answer: 5**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-40.title: Poisson limit
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-40.body:
By linearity $\frac{c(n)}n$ is the probability that a given person receives at least $5$ votes. The probability of exactly $k$ votes is
$$\binom nk\left(\frac1n\right)^k\left(\frac{n-1}n\right)^{n-k}=\left(\frac{n-1}n\right)^n\cdot\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{k!\,(n-1)^k}\longrightarrow\frac1{e\cdot k!}.$$
Hence the limit is
$$1-\frac1e\left(\frac1{0!}+\frac1{1!}+\frac1{2!}+\frac1{3!}+\frac1{4!}\right)=1-\frac{65}{24e}.$$

**Answer: $1-\dfrac{65}{24e}$**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-41.title: Periodic jump sequences
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-41.body:
Label the stones $0,\dots,41$ (mod $42$). A valid route leaves each stone exactly once and enters each stone exactly once, so each stone $n$ has a jump length $r_n\in\{1,7\}$. If $r_n=7$ the route enters $n+7$ from $n$, so stone $n+6$ cannot jump $1$ to $n+7$: $r_{n+6}=7$. Hence $r_n=7\Rightarrow r_{n+6}=7\Rightarrow\cdots$, and going around the (length-$7$) cycle $n,n+6,\dots,n+36$ all of these stones have $r=7$. So $r_n$ depends only on $n\bmod6$: $r_n=f(n\bmod 6)$ for some $f:\mathbb Z_6\to\{1,7\}$, at most $2^6=64$ choices.

Every jump is $\equiv1\pmod6$, so the jumps made from six consecutive positions of the route use $f$ on all six residues: each block of six consecutive jumps has the same total $\ell=\sum_\rho f(\rho)=6+6t$, where $t$ is the number of $7$'s in $f$. If $t=6$ the route returns after $6$ jumps: invalid. For $0\le t\le5$ suppose the route visits some stone twice among its first $42$ positions: $s_i=s_j$, $0\le i<j<42$. Since $s_j\equiv s_i+(j-i)\pmod6$, $j-i=6k$ with $1\le k\le6$, and $k\ell\equiv0\pmod{42}$, i.e. $6k(1+t)\equiv0\pmod{42}$, so $7\mid k(1+t)$ with $1\le k\le6$, $1\le1+t\le6$: impossible. So the $42$ positions $s_0,\dots,s_{41}$ are distinct stones, and $s_{42}=s_0+7\ell\equiv s_0$, so the route is valid.

So exactly the $63$ functions $f$ other than “all $7$” work.

**Answer: 63**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-42.title: Empty boxes first
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-42.body:
Each row and column holds exactly $3$ balls, so exactly one box in each row and column is empty: $4!=24$ choices. Relabel rows so that the empty boxes form the diagonal. Six purple balls and four rows: each row has $2$ purple $+1$ green or $1$ purple $+2$ green, so exactly two rows have two purple balls; there are $\binom42=6$ choices of those rows, and by symmetry we may count with rows $1,2$ being the “two purple” rows (rows $3,4$ have one purple, two green).

Write $M$ for the $4\times4$ zero-diagonal $0/1$ matrix of purple positions. Its row sums are $(2,2,1,1)$, its total is $6$, and every column sum must be $1$ or $2$, hence exactly two columns have sum $2$. Enumerating by the column-sum vector:

| column sums | $(1,1,2,2)$ | $(1,2,1,2)$ | $(2,1,1,2)$ | $(1,2,2,1)$ | $(2,1,2,1)$ | $(2,2,1,1)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| matrices | $8$ | $6$ | $6$ | $6$ | $6$ | $4$ |

for a total of $36$. Therefore the number of arrangements is $24\cdot6\cdot36=5184$.

**Answer: 5184**

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-43.title: How this round is scored
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-43.body:
This is a game against the other teams, not a question with one correct answer. Writing $N$ scores $N$ points only if at least $N$ teams (including you) wrote $N$. Writing a large number is risky because few other teams will pick the same one; writing $1$ scores $1$ point always (at least $1$ team, yours, wrote $1$). The official solutions remark: “Well, maybe you can get $1$ point.”

Practice mode: pick a number, compare with others if you play in a group, and score yourself.

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-44.title: A known example
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-44.body: This is Znam's problem (1972). The smallest known example is $S=\{2,3,11,23,31\}$: here $P=47058$ and $\frac P2+1=23530=2\cdot11765$, $\frac P3+1=15687=3\cdot5229$, $\frac P{11}+1=4279=11\cdot389$, $\frac P{23}+1=2047=23\cdot89$, $\frac P{31}+1=1519=31\cdot49$; in each case $x$ divides $\frac Px+1$ and is smaller than it, so $x$ is a proper divisor. This set has $n=5$ and scores $10$. A set with $7$ elements is $S=\{2,3,11,17,101,149,3109\}$ (score $14$). Solutions exist for $|S|\ge5$, but explicit ones have been found only for $|S|\le13$.

hmmt-feb-2005-guts-45.title: An example
hmmt-feb-2005-guts-45.body:
Square subwords here are blocks $uu$ of consecutive letters, and every occurrence counts. Searching with a computer (extending words letter by letter and keeping those with the fewest squares), the word
$$01001101000110010110001101001100010110011101001101$$
has length $n=50$ and contains $s=25$ occurrences of square subwords, so it scores $50-25=25$, which is close to the best possible (the maximum score is of order $25$; asymptotically the minimum number of squares in a word of length $n$ is about $0.551n$).
